components.summary: Outlined uppercase chip naming a discrete thing — a category, skill, filter or chosen value. Static, interactive, latched or removable.

props.name: variant
props.description:
Emphasis level. `default` is the standard visible outline (alt text,
muted-foreground border) that reads correctly standalone — use it for skill
chips and most labels. `subtle` is a quieter treatment (muted text,
elevated-border) for dense or secondary contexts.

props.name: interactive
props.description:
Makes the chip body a real button — focusable, with Enter and Space. The
accent border and label come with it. Reflected.

props.name: pressed
props.description:
Latched state for a filter chip; sets aria-pressed and fills the chip.
Implies interactive. Controlled by the consumer — the chip does not toggle
itself, so flip it on the click event. Reflected.

props.name: removable
props.description:
Adds a trailing dismiss control that fires rr-chip-remove. Independent of
interactive: a static value chip can be removable. Reflected.

props.name: empty
props.description:
Renders the awaiting-input treatment — dashed edge, muted label — for a
chip acting as a trigger with nothing chosen yet. Distinct from disabled:
an empty chip is still operable. Reflected.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables the chip body and its dismiss control. Reflected.

props.name: removeLabel
props.description:
Accessible name for the dismiss control. Name the thing being removed
("Remove Income filter") — a row of chips all saying "Remove" tells a
screen-reader user nothing. Maps to attribute remove-label.

slots.name: default
slots.description: Chip label text. Rendered uppercase via CSS — pass normal-case text.

slots.name: leading
slots.description: Icon or marker before the label, inside the chip's own padding rhythm.

slots.name: trailing
slots.description: Icon or marker after the label. Not the remove control — that is the removable prop.

events.name: rr-chip-remove
events.detail: Bubbles (composed) when the dismiss control is activated. Not fired while disabled. The chip does not remove itself — the consumer decides what happens.

cssParts.name: chip
cssParts.description: The outer chip container that carries the border, fill and radius.

cssParts.name: body
cssParts.description: The label body — a button when interactive or pressed, a span otherwise.

cssParts.name: remove
cssParts.description: The dismiss control, a sibling of the body rather than a child.

rules.rule: No hardcoded colors — use var(--color-*) custom properties
Accent green (foreground.action, foreground.accent, background.action, background.accent) is never resting text or decoration — it signals interactivity or intentional emphasis only
All text must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) against its background — all pairings in the system already do; do not introduce new ones without checking
Never use primitive tokens (color.green.*, space.*, font.size.*) in UI code — always go through the semantic layer

Motion must respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (WCAG 2.3.3). The built brand CSS zeroes `--motion-duration-*` under `reduce`, so token-driven transitions stop automatically — never hardcode a transition/animation duration that bypasses the tokens. Any infinite animation (spin, shimmer, pulse) cannot be reached by the token override and MUST carry its own `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` guard that stops or damps it

guidance: Chip vs badge is a question of provenance, not interactivity. A badge reports state the system decided and you cannot influence — status, count, validity. A chip names a discrete thing — a category, a skill, a filter, a value someone chose. Pick by asking who decided what it says, not by whether it is clickable.

A chip keeps ONE silhouette in every mode: radius.sm, interactive or not (owner's call, 2026-09-03). What changes is the affordance — an operable chip earns the accent, a focus ring and Enter/Space. Never change the radius to signal interactivity; a reader of a mock could not then tell an interactive chip from a wrong one.

pressed implies interactive, and is CONTROLLED — the chip does not toggle itself, exactly like rr-tab[selected]. Listen for click and flip the prop. A chip that toggled itself would fight every consumer holding filter state of its own.

removable is independent of interactive: a static value chip can carry a dismiss control. The control is a SIBLING of the body, never a child — a button inside a button is neither valid HTML nor operable — and its click is stopped so it cannot also read as a click on the chip.
Name what the dismiss control removes via remove-label ("Remove Income filter"). A row of chips all announcing "Remove" tells a screen-reader user nothing about which one they are on.

empty is awaiting-input, NOT disabled. It keeps a legible dashed border and stays fully operable; disabled recedes to near-canvas and stops accepting input. Reaching for disabled to mean "nothing chosen yet" tells the user the control is unavailable when it is in fact the next thing they should press.

When a chip is used as the trigger for a popup, it must not declare aria-haspopup or aria-expanded itself. The popup stamps those onto whatever sits in its trigger slot, exactly as rr-menu already does — so the same chip stays correct when it is used as a plain filter.

Do not point a chip border at --color-border-default for the resting state: it equals background.alt and disappears on the page canvas. The default variant uses foreground.muted and the subtle variant uses border.elevated so both stay visible standalone. (empty is the deliberate exception — a dashed border.default edge reads as an unfilled field.)
Content is transformed to uppercase with --letter-spacing-all-caps in CSS; authors pass normal-case text and must not pre-uppercase it.

keyboard: Tab reaches the chip body when interactive or pressed, and the dismiss control when removable
Enter and Space activate the body and the dismiss control, via native buttons
rules: Chip text alone must convey meaning; do not rely on the border or emphasis level to communicate.
A static chip exposes NO role and is not focusable — it renders a span. Only interactive, pressed and removable introduce controls, and each is a native button so Enter and Space come for free.
aria-pressed is present only when pressed, and absent entirely otherwise — an unpressed toggle and a plain button are different things to a screen reader.
The dismiss control carries its own accessible name via remove-label; name the value being removed, not the action alone.
empty stays operable and keeps a legible edge. Never use disabled to mean "nothing chosen yet": disabled removes the control from the tab order and announces it as unavailable.

Both variants meet WCAG AA for text contrast on the base canvas (default 8.0:1, subtle 6.3:1). Interactive uses foreground.action (11.1:1 on canvas, 9.0:1 on background.alt hover); pressed pairs foreground.accent-green on background.accent-green at 9.7:1.
A chip used as a popup trigger must not declare aria-haspopup or aria-expanded — the popup owns those.

components.name: rr-listbox
components.summary: Selection popover (WAI-ARIA listbox pattern) for choosing one value from rich options — icons, descriptions and a selected check.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the listbox is open. Usually driven by the component itself; settable for controlled usage.

props.name: placement
props.description: Which edge of the trigger the listbox aligns to: bottom-start (default) or bottom-end.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the listbox popup (required); sets aria-label on the role=listbox element.

props.name: value
props.description: The chosen option's value. Owned by the component; set it to control the selection.

slots.name: trigger
slots.description: The control that opens the listbox — an rr-chip, because the trigger displays the current value.

events.name: rr-listbox-select
events.detail: Fired when an option is chosen; detail.value is the option's value.

events.name: rr-listbox-toggle
events.detail: Fired when the listbox opens or closes; detail.open is the new state.

rules.rule: No hardcoded colors — use var(--color-*) custom properties
Accent green (foreground.action, foreground.accent, background.action, background.accent) is never resting text or decoration — it signals interactivity or intentional emphasis only
All text must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) against its background — all pairings in the system already do; do not introduce new ones without checking
Never use primitive tokens (color.green.*, space.*, font.size.*) in UI code — always go through the semantic layer

guidance: Listbox vs menu is a question of what the control DOES, not how it looks. A menu fires commands and nothing latches; a listbox sets a value and the chosen option stays marked. Using rr-menu for selection is the wrong ARIA role, not merely a missing prop — role=menuitem has no selected state at all.

Listbox vs rr-select is a question of option content. rr-select wraps a native <select> and emits native <option>, which renders text and nothing else at any level of CSS effort — that constraint is the platform's, and it is what makes rr-select form-associated. Reach for rr-listbox only when an option needs an icon, a swatch or a second line; reach for rr-select whenever plain text will do, because it participates in forms for free.

The trigger is an rr-chip and the menu trigger is an rr-button. Those two silhouettes — radius.sm against radius.default — are the only cue distinguishing them at rest, since both are 'click a thing, a panel appears'. A chip is right here because what the trigger displays IS the current value. Use the chip's empty mode while nothing is chosen.

Never let the trigger declare aria-haspopup or aria-expanded itself: the listbox stamps both onto whatever sits in the trigger slot, exactly as rr-menu does. That is what keeps one chip correct as a filter and as a trigger.

value is OWNED by the listbox and settable to control it — unlike rr-chip[pressed] and rr-tab[selected], which are controlled only. The line is whether the component can see the whole state: a listbox holds exactly one value and is the container for it, while a chip is one control in a filter row whose state is the set, which no single chip can know.

Opening focuses the CURRENT value, not the first option — reopening a listbox should put you where you already are. A list that always opens at the top makes the user re-find their own choice every time.
Always set label; it names the popup for assistive tech. The popup positions with CSS below the trigger (no portal), so keep the listbox outside overflow:hidden ancestors.

  <rr-option value="income">Income</rr-option>

ArrowDown or ArrowUp on the trigger opens it focused on the current value
ArrowDown/ArrowUp move through enabled options and wrap; Home/End jump to the ends
Enter or Space chooses the focused option, closes, and returns focus to the trigger
Escape closes and returns focus to the trigger; Tab closes and moves on

Every option carries aria-selected, true or false — a listbox whose unchosen options are silent reads as a list of buttons

The selected option is marked by a check glyph as well as accent colour, so selection never depends on colour alone

All text must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) against its background — all pairings in the system already do; do not introduce new ones without checking

The built brand CSS zeroes `--motion-duration-*` under `reduce`, so token-driven transitions stop automatically — never hardcode a transition/animation duration that bypasses the tokens. A description is a second line of meaning, not a place for overflow. If the label needs the description to make sense, the label is wrong.

rules: aria-selected is present on every option, true or false, not only on the chosen one
Disabled options carry aria-disabled and are inert to both click and keyboard
Selection is carried by a check glyph as well as accent colour — never by colour alone
The focused row shows an inset focus ring, because options are focused programmatically inside an overlay

components.summary: One choice inside rr-segmented. Carries its label colour only — the parent draws the sliding indicator.

props.description: The value this segment commits to the group when chosen. Reflected.

props.name: selected
props.description: Marks the chosen segment. Set by the parent rr-segmented — do not set directly. Reflected.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Prevents selection and skips this segment during arrow navigation. Reflected.

props.name: tone
props.description:
Semantic colour this choice carries once selected — the label takes the
matching foreground and the parent tints the indicator to match. Reflected.

props.name: tabStop
props.description:
Marks this segment as the group's single tab stop (roving tabindex). Set
by the parent rr-segmented — do not set directly. Maps to attribute tab-stop.

slots.name: default
slots.description: Segment label text (and optional leading icon).

events.name: rr-segment-select
events.detail: Bubbles (composed) to rr-segmented when the segment is clicked; detail.value is this segment's value. Not fired when disabled or already selected.

rules.rule: No hardcoded colors — use var(--color-*) custom properties
All text must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) against its background — all pairings in the system already do; do not introduce new ones without checking
Never use primitive tokens (color.green.*, space.*, font.size.*) in UI code — always go through the semantic layer

Motion must respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (WCAG 2.3.3). The built brand CSS zeroes `--motion-duration-*` under `reduce`, so token-driven transitions stop automatically — never hardcode a transition/animation duration that bypasses the tokens. Any infinite animation (spin, shimmer, pulse) cannot be reached by the token override and MUST carry its own `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` guard that stops or damps it

guidance: Do not set selected or tab-stop directly — control the chosen segment via rr-segmented[value]. Both are written by the parent on every sync.

A segment paints no chrome of its own: no fill, no border, no shadow. That restraint is the component — two segments that each drew a box would read as two adjacent buttons instead of one field with one value.

tone colours the label when this segment is chosen, and the parent lifts the same tone onto the indicator. The set is neutral, success and danger only: a two- or three-choice control can carry a binary verdict (approve/deny, pass/fail, on/off) and nothing more. warning and info are message roles — they describe something the system is telling you, not a choice someone made. A third outcome that genuinely needs its own colour (decision-engine's Review) should get its own tone added deliberately, not borrow a feedback role.

keyboard: Enter or Space activates the focused segment via its native button
Arrow keys are handled by the parent rr-segmented, not here
rules: aria-checked and the roving tabindex are managed in concert with rr-segmented.
Host uses delegatesFocus so focus forwards to the inner button.
The focus ring is inset rather than outset: the segment sits inside the track's rounded edge, where an outset outline would be clipped.

Unselected labels use foreground.muted, which clears AA on the track (6.3:1 base dark) — the system's sub-AA foreground.inactive is decision-engine-only chrome and is deliberately not used here (#232).

components.name: rr-segmented
components.summary: A field whose two or three choices are all visible at rest — a radiogroup with a sliding indicator, not a row of buttons.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible label for the group (required); sets aria-label on the radiogroup.

props.name: value
props.description: The chosen segment's value. Empty means nothing is chosen and no indicator is drawn. Reflected.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables the whole group and every segment in it. Reflected.

events.name: change
events.detail: Fired (bubbles, composed) when the value changes by click or keyboard; detail.value is the newly chosen segment's value.

cssParts.name: track
cssParts.description: The outer track the segments sit in.

cssParts.name: indicator
cssParts.description: The sliding pill drawn behind the chosen segment. Absent when nothing is chosen.

rules.rule: No hardcoded colors — use var(--color-*) custom properties
All text must meet WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1) against its background — all pairings in the system already do; do not introduce new ones without checking
Never use primitive tokens (color.green.*, space.*, font.size.*) in UI code — always go through the semantic layer

Motion must respect `prefers-reduced-motion` (WCAG 2.3.3). The built brand CSS zeroes `--motion-duration-*` under `reduce`, so token-driven transitions stop automatically — never hardcode a transition/animation duration that bypasses the tokens. Any infinite animation (spin, shimmer, pulse) cannot be reached by the token override and MUST carry its own `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` guard that stops or damps it

guidance: Use it at two or three choices. Past that the control stops fitting and the choice belongs behind a click — reach for a listbox instead. This is the same job as a listbox (set a field's value), traded for screen space.

It is a field, not a row of buttons and not a menu: exactly one choice is checked and the value survives the interaction. A menu latches nothing; a chip group names things rather than setting one value.
Leave value empty for an unanswered field — no indicator is drawn at all, so a draft row cannot be mistaken for one that chose the first option.

Segments are equal-width by construction (one 1fr grid column each, so every segment is as wide as the widest label), which is what lets the indicator be placed arithmetically instead of measured. Labels of very different lengths will make the whole control wide; shorten the labels rather than fighting the layout.
The indicator owns all the chrome — fill, border, shadow. Never give a segment its own box: two boxed segments read as two adjacent buttons rather than one field.

Set tone on a segment to colour-code the chosen value; the indicator picks up a 12% tint of the same role. That is what makes an outcome scannable down a column of many rows. Only neutral, success and danger exist, because a two- or three-choice control can only carry a binary verdict.
The pill slides on motion-easing-move. An overshoot curve would read better — the pill should feel moved rather than recoloured — but the system has no spring easing yet (#232).

  <rr-segment value="deny" tone="danger">Deny</rr-segment>

keyboard: Tab enters the group once — the chosen segment is the tab stop, or the first enabled one when nothing is chosen
ArrowRight / ArrowDown move to the next enabled segment and select it (wraps)
ArrowLeft / ArrowUp move to the previous enabled segment and select it (wraps)
Home selects the first enabled segment, End the last
With nothing chosen, either arrow direction commits the first segment
rules: label is required so the radiogroup has an accessible name via aria-label.
Selection follows focus, per the WAI-ARIA radio group pattern: arrows both move and check. Roving tabindex keeps the whole group to one tab stop.
The indicator is a non-text state indicator under SC 1.4.11: it carries a border at color-border-default (3:1+ on the track) as well as its fill, so the chosen segment is not signalled by fill alone.
Tone is never the only channel — the chosen segment is also the one the pill sits under and the only one with aria-checked=true.
Tinted pills are color-mix composites the contrast gate cannot declare as a pairing. Measured on base dark against their tone foreground: success 6.9:1, danger 5.5:1, neutral 9.9:1 — all AA.

declarations.description:
An outlined, uppercase chip — a discrete thing: a category, a skill, a
filter, a value someone chose.

The deliberate counterpart to `<rr-badge>`, and the line between them is
**provenance, not interactivity**: a badge reports state the *system* decided
and you cannot influence (status, count, validity); a chip names a thing. So
the badge is a filled pill and the chip is a square-cornered (radius.sm),
bordered label. Content is rendered UPPERCASE with all-caps letter-spacing,
so authors pass normal-case text.

**A chip keeps one silhouette in every mode.** Interactive or not, it is
`radius.sm` (owner's call, 2026-09-03). What changes is the *affordance*:
an operable chip earns the accent, a focus ring and Enter/Space, exactly as
hard rule 5 describes. A component that changed shape on a boolean would put
the same object in a design file under two outlines, and nobody reading a
mock could tell "this chip is interactive" from "someone used the wrong
radius".

Four modes compose freely:

- **static** (default) — no role, not focusable. A label.
- **`interactive`** — the body becomes a real `<button>`; click, Enter and
  Space all work, and `click` bubbles from the host.
- **`pressed`** — a latched filter chip (`aria-pressed`). Implies
  `interactive`. **Controlled, not self-toggling**: like `rr-tab[selected]`,
  the consumer owns the state and flips it on `click`.
- **`removable`** — a trailing dismiss button, a *sibling* of the body
  rather than a child, because a button inside a button is neither valid
  HTML nor a usable control. Fires `rr-chip-remove`.

`empty` is the "nothing chosen yet" treatment for a chip used as a trigger:
a dashed edge and muted text. It must read as **awaiting input**, never as
disabled — so it stays fully operable and keeps a legible border, where
`disabled` recedes to near-canvas and stops accepting input.

Used as a popup trigger, a chip **never declares `aria-haspopup` or
`aria-expanded` itself** — the popup stamps those onto whatever sits in its
trigger slot, as `rr-menu` already does (`menu.ts:148-149`). That is what
keeps one chip correct both as a trigger and as a plain filter.

Uses semantic design tokens for all visual properties. Brand theming
cascades automatically via CSS custom properties on `:root`.

declarations.description:
`<rr-segment>` — one choice inside `<rr-segmented>`.

Selection state is owned by the parent: it sets `selected` and `tab-stop`,
and it draws the sliding indicator. **A segment paints no chrome of its
own** — no fill, no border, no shadow — only its label colour. That is the
whole reason this is a component rather than a row of chips: two segments
that each drew their own box would read as two adjacent buttons, not as one
field with one value.

`tone` colours the label when this segment is the selected one, and the
parent lifts the same tone onto the indicator so the pill is tinted to
match. It is how an outcome stays scannable down a column of many rows.

The set is deliberately only `success` and `danger` beside `neutral`: this
control holds two or three choices, so the only colour-coding it can carry
is a binary verdict — approve/deny, pass/fail, on/off. `warning` and `info`
are message roles; they describe something the system is telling you, not a
choice someone made, and offering them here just invites arbitrary colour.

declarations.description:
`<rr-segmented>` — a segmented control: a field whose two or three choices
are all visible at rest.

It does the same job as a listbox — **set a field's value** — but spends
screen space instead of a click. That trade only pays at two or three
options; past that it stops fitting and the choice belongs behind a click.

The tell that it is a field and not a row of buttons: `role="radiogroup"` /
`role="radio"`, exactly one choice checked, and a value that survives the
interaction. A menu, by contrast, latches nothing.

**The sliding pill is the whole design.** One absolutely-positioned
indicator carries the fill, border and shadow and translates between
segments; the segments themselves carry only semantic text colour. Segments
are equal-width — one `1fr` grid column each, so every segment is as wide as
the widest label — which is what lets the indicator be placed arithmetically
rather than measured.

With no value set, **no indicator is drawn at all** — a draft row that has
not been answered must not look like it picked the first option.
declarations.name: RrSegmented

declarations.description:
`<rr-table>` — a structural data table composed from `rr-table-row` and
`rr-table-cell`.

Raw `<tr>`/`<td>` can't be slotted into a custom element (the HTML parser
drops table tags outside a `<table>` context), so the family uses CSS
table display with explicit ARIA table semantics: this host is the

buttons.

every table in the system shares one visual language. The hover tint only
renders when `interactive` is set — accent green signals interactivity,
